t: Shinto, “the way of the kami”, is the native religion of Japan: the worship of the kami, the sacred powers present in mountains, trees, rivers, ancestors and great people, at shrines across the country, with no founder and no single scripture.

For a thousand years kami and buddhas were worshipped together, until the Meiji government separated them in 1868 and built a State Shinto around the divine emperor, which the Allied occupation dismantled in 1945.

Today festivals, New Year shrine visits and rites of passage keep Shinto at the heart of Japanese life, while its shrines, rituals and reverence for nature have shaped the country’s art and architecture.
dyk: The Grand Shrine of Ise has been rebuilt in identical form on a neighbouring site every twenty years since 690, apart from a long interruption during the civil wars of the 15th and 16th centuries: the 62nd rebuilding was completed in 2013.

f.origin: Japan, with roots in prehistoric times; named and organised around the imperial court from the 7th and 8th centuries
f.founder: None: it grew from the rites of Japan’s communities and clans
f.scriptures: No single scripture; the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720) record its myths, and the Engishiki (927) its rites and prayers
f.followers: Most Japanese take part in its festivals and rites at some 80,000 shrines, though few call Shinto their religion
